fix: Serve each accepted web connection on the mux, or on a bounded worker pool that ACL2 admits, the way the control plane admits its workers (fn-ncla-launch-disposition). Turn :defer and the cursor resume into timers, not sleep calls on a shared thread.
reviewer: web-host.lisp:310-322 runs a single thread that accepts and then calls fnn-web-serve inline, so the next accept waits until the current connection finishes. fnn-web-serve calls fnn-tls-accept with a 10 s timeout (line 271), and the request then runs synchronously. fnn-web-feed sleeps up to 1 s on :defer (line 113) and sleeps the cursor-resume time on a yield (line 124), both on that same thread. The listen backlog is 64 (line 302). An idle or slow client therefore blocks every other web user for the handshake and request deadlines. The NNTP mux is not affected, so this is a denial of the optional web face only.
scenario: An unauthenticated remote client opens a TCP connection to the public web port and sends nothing, or does a slow TLS handshake. The accept thread is inside fnn-web-serve for up to 10 s (handshake) plus 15 s (request deadline). After that, each 10-second send to a reader that is not reading also blocks it. Every other browser waits in the 64-entry backlog the whole time. Looping that connection is a cheap, permanent denial of the web face, which ember describes as the node's own reader. A legitimate user whose address has run out of its exposure budget also makes the thread sleep up to 1 s per deferral (fnn-web-feed :defer) while every other user waits. A cursor yield in a long render does the same. The NNTP side runs on a nonblocking mux, but the web side is serial and blocking.
title: The web face serves one connection at a time on its only thread, and that thread also sleeps for exposure charges
